claims.text: Replacing conventional EAM references with a machine-learned interatomic potential will improve reference–target phase-space overlap in high-entropy alloys near melting.
A machine-learned reference will reduce thermodynamic-integration path mismatch relative to TOR-TILD calculations using EAM references.
The proposed potential would be trained on extensive ab initio databases containing diverse solid and liquid configurations.
The machine-learned potential would serve as the reference potential in thermodynamic integration within a TOR-TILD-type framework.
The intervention is applicable to near-equimolar high-entropy alloys containing four or more components.
The applicable temperature range is approximately 0.95 Tm to Tm.
Near melting, the ab initio liquid exhibits a large diversity of atomic configurations.
Machine-learned potentials can capture many-body interactions and diverse local atomic environments in the liquid state.
Capturing many-body interactions and diverse local environments improves phase-space overlap between the reference model and the ab initio target.
Training on both solid and liquid ab initio configurations allows the ML potential to represent the local energy landscape and configurational variability more accurately.
A more accurate representation of the local energy landscape smooths the thermodynamic-integration path.
EAM potentials are limited in their ability to capture many-body effects in disordered high-temperature states.
Standard EAM references have poor phase-space overlap with the ab initio liquid because they inadequately represent its possible atomic configurations.
The ML reference is predicted to reduce thermodynamic-integration path mismatch by approximately 40–50% relative to TOR-TILD EAM references.
Reducing path mismatch will produce more reliable free-energy calculations.
Performance may degrade outside the near-equimolar composition space or near-melting temperature window.
Performance may degrade when sufficient machine-learning training data are unavailable.
The magnitude of improvement depends on the alloy system and the quality of ML training.
